question: A patient presents with sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward. Which diagnosis primarily involves inflammation of the fibrous sac surrounding the heart?
cited_learning_objective: Define the Pericardium and list the Disease Presentations associated with Pericardial Disease.

options.text: Acute inflammation of the pericardial sac pericarditis
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture defines acute pericarditis as inflammation of the pericardial sac and lists it as the primary pericardial disease.

options.text: Ischemic necrosis of myocardium from coronary occlusion
options.rationale: Wrong: Myocardial infarction affects heart muscle due to coronary occlusion; it would be correct only if the primary pathology were myocardial ischemia rather than sac inflammation.

options.text: Thromboembolic obstruction of pulmonary arterial vasculature
options.rationale: Wrong: Pulmonary embolism involves pulmonary arteries and not the pericardial sac; it would be correct only if the fibrous sac were secondarily inflamed.

options.text: Intimal tear with mediastinal hemorrhage aortic dissection
options.rationale: Wrong: Aortic dissection is an aortic wall tear; it does not primarily inflame the pericardial sac and would be correct only if dissection caused tamponade with sac involvement.

options.text: Infectious consolidation of lung parenchyma lobar pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong: Pneumonia affects lung tissue rather than the pericardial sac; it would be correct only if pleuropericardial spread produced sac inflammation.

question: Which two clinical findings together meet the diagnostic threshold when evaluating a patient suspected of inflammation of the heart's outer covering?
cited_learning_objective: Acute Pericarditis – Diagnostic Criteria (Need 2 out of 4)

options.text: Pleuritic chest pain and a superficial scratchy friction rub
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists chest pain and pericardial friction rub as two of the four diagnostic criteria; two of four are required for diagnosis.

options.text: Fever above 38 C and elevated blood glucose level
options.rationale: Wrong: Fever may occur but elevated glucose is not a diagnostic criterion; this would be correct only if glucose were listed as a criterion in the lecture.

options.text: Localized dull chest pain and focal pulmonary crackles
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericarditis pain is sharp and pleuritic and crackles suggest pulmonary disease; this would be correct only if exam findings matched pericardial inflammation.

options.text: New focal ST depression on ECG and hemoptysis present
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture cites widespread ST elevation or PR depression, not focal ST depression; hemoptysis is unrelated and would need to be absent for pericarditis diagnosis.

options.text: Isolated cardiomegaly on chest radiograph without symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericardial effusion can be a criterion but isolated radiographic cardiomegaly without clinical features would not meet the two-criterion requirement.

question: A young adult with pleuritic chest pain has diffuse ST elevation and PR depression on ECG. Which diagnostic test is class I recommended in all such cases to assess for fluid around the heart?

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography to evaluate pericardial effusion
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states echocardiography is a Class I recommendation in all cases to assess pericardial effusion.

options.text: Routine coronary angiography to visualize coronary arteries
options.rationale: Wrong: Cardiac catheterization is used mainly to exclude ischemic disease, not as a universal first-line test for pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if ischemia were strongly suspected.

options.text: High-resolution chest CT to evaluate pulmonary parenchyma
options.rationale: Wrong: Chest CT is not the class I test for pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if CT were specifically indicated for alternative diagnoses.

options.text: Transesophageal echocardiography for routine pericardial screening
options.rationale: Wrong: TEE is not the routine class I test; transthoracic echo is preferred unless TEE is specifically indicated.

options.text: Cardiac MRI with gadolinium for all suspected cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Cardiac MRI is selective per the lecture and not class I in all cases; it would be correct only in selected situations.

question: Which medication combination is recommended for most patients with presumed idiopathic or viral inflammation of the heart's outer layers?

options.text: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory plus colchicine combination therapy
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends combination therapy with NSAIDs plus colchicine for most idiopathic or viral acute pericarditis.

options.text: High-dose systemic corticosteroids as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Steroids are reserved for specific causes like connective tissue disease; they would be correct only if pericarditis were due to SLE or uremia.

options.text: Anticoagulation with warfarin for all pericarditis patients
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticoagulation is not routine for pericarditis; it would be correct only if there were LV thrombus, AF, or very low LVEF per the lecture.

options.text: Routine intravenous antibiotics for presumed viral cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Bacterial therapy is indicated only with suspected bacterial etiology; routine antibiotics are inappropriate for presumed viral pericarditis.

options.text: Immediate pericardiectomy for initial symptom control
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgical pericardiectomy is reserved for constriction or refractory cases; it would be correct only if medical therapy failed or constrictive physiology were present.

question: A patient with recurrent symptomatic inflammation of the pericardial sac despite NSAIDs is most likely to benefit from which adjunctive therapy that reduces recurrence risk by about half?

options.text: Oral colchicine added to anti-inflammatory therapy for recurrence reduction
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture cites colchicine reduces recurrence by about 50% and is recommended adjunctive therapy.

options.text: Long-term low-dose corticosteroids to prevent future episodes
options.rationale: Wrong: Steroids are used mainly for connective tissue disease or uremia; they would be correct only if the pericarditis were steroid-responsive autoimmune disease.

options.text: Chronic anticoagulation to prevent inflammatory recurrences
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticoagulation does not prevent pericarditis recurrence; it would be correct only if thromboembolic complications were present.

options.text: Routine pericardial window creation to reduce recurrence risk
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgical drainage is for large effusions, tamponade, or refractory cases; it would be correct only if effusions were recurrent and symptomatic despite medical therapy.

options.text: Daily colchicine monotherapy without NSAID coadministration
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture recommends colchicine with NSAIDs for acute cases; colchicine alone would be correct only if NSAIDs were contraindicated.

question: Which of the following is the most critical alternative diagnosis to exclude immediately because its treatment differs and delay increases mortality when evaluating chest pain that could be pericardial in origin?
cited_learning_objective: Differential Diagnosis of Acute Pericarditis – Includes ALL causes of Chest Pain

options.text: Acute aortic dissection requiring urgent vascular intervention
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture emphasizes ruling out aortic dissection because it has high morbidity and requires different urgent management.

options.text: Viral upper respiratory infection managed conservatively at home
options.rationale: Wrong: URIs are less emergent and not the critical high-mortality mimic; this would be correct only if symptoms were limited to upper airway without chest signs.

options.text: Stable chronic angina managed with outpatient risk modification
options.rationale: Wrong: Stable angina is not the immediate high-risk mimic; it would be correct only if exertional chest pain without acute features were present.

options.text: Musculoskeletal chest wall strain treated with analgesics and rest
options.rationale: Wrong: Musculoskeletal pain is a benign mimic; it would be correct only if reproducible chest wall tenderness and absence of systemic signs were documented.

options.text: Community-acquired pneumonia requiring oral antibiotics
options.rationale: Wrong: Pneumonia can mimic pleuritic pain but is not the highest-risk diagnosis to exclude emergently; it would be correct only if focal pulmonary findings and imaging supported pneumonia.

question: A patient with suspected pericardial inflammation has normal serial high-sensitivity troponin I values. According to the lecture, which interpretation aligns best with these biomarker results?

options.text: Myocardial necrosis is unlikely; isolated pericardial inflammation probable
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes normal serial hs-troponins suggest absence of myocardial injury and support isolated pericarditis.

options.text: Fulminant myocarditis is confirmed despite normal biomarkers
options.rationale: Wrong: Fulminant myocarditis often has myocardial injury and hemodynamic compromise; normal troponins would not confirm it.

options.text: Cardiac tamponade is present regardless of troponin levels
options.rationale: Wrong: Tamponade is a hemodynamic state diagnosed by exam and echo; troponin levels alone do not establish tamponade.

options.text: Ischemic myocardial infarction is proven absent in all cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Normal troponins make MI less likely but do not absolutely exclude ischemia early; serial testing and clinical context are required.

options.text: Pericardial effusion size can be estimated from troponin values
options.rationale: Wrong: Troponins do not quantify effusion; echocardiography is required to assess effusion size.

question: Which imaging modality has sensitivity around 76% and specificity around 96% for detecting myocardial inflammation with gadolinium enhancement, per the lecture?

options.text: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium enhancement
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture reports cardiac MRI with gadolinium has ~76% sensitivity and ~96% specificity for myocarditis.

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography assessing wall motion abnormalities
options.rationale: Wrong: Echo is useful but the lecture gives the sensitivity and specificity figures specifically for cardiac MRI, not echo.

options.text: Chest radiograph demonstrating cardiomegaly and congestion
options.rationale: Wrong: Chest X-ray findings vary and do not match the cited sensitivity/specificity metrics for myocarditis imaging.

options.text: Coronary angiography excluding obstructive coronary disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Cath is used to exclude ischemia but does not provide the stated sensitivity/specificity for myocardial inflammation.

options.text: Transesophageal echocardiography for detailed valvular assessment
options.rationale: Wrong: TEE evaluates valves and structures but is not the modality with the reported MRI diagnostic performance.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis presents with new heart failure and cardiogenic shock. According to the lecture, which invasive diagnostic procedure should be considered because it can identify treatable specific etiologies?
cited_learning_objective: When should Endomyocardial Biopsy (EMB) be performed?

options.text: Endomyocardial biopsy to identify specific inflammatory etiologies
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends EMB in fulminant myocarditis to diagnose conditions like giant cell or eosinophilic myocarditis that have specific therapies.

options.text: Immediate pericardiocentesis to relieve myocardial inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericardiocentesis treats effusion/tamponade, not diagnostic myocardial biopsy; it would be correct only if tamponade were present.

options.text: Electrophysiology study to map ventricular arrhythmias
options.rationale: Wrong: EP study addresses arrhythmias but does not provide histologic diagnosis; it would be correct only if arrhythmia management required mapping.

options.text: Coronary angiography to confirm myocarditis etiology
options.rationale: Wrong: Angiography excludes ischemic causes but cannot histologically diagnose myocarditis; it would be correct only to rule out ischemia.

options.text: Right heart catheterization to measure pulmonary pressures
options.rationale: Wrong: Hemodynamic assessment may be useful but does not identify specific inflammatory etiologies treatable with targeted therapy.

question: Which pathogen group is listed in the lecture as a common cause of myocarditis in developed countries?
cited_learning_objective: In Developed Countries – Most Common Causes

options.text: Enteroviruses such as Coxsackie B causing viral myocarditis
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists enteroviruses, including Coxsackie B, among the most common viral causes in developed countries.

options.text: Trypanosoma cruzi infection causing chronic myocarditis
options.rationale: Wrong: Chagas disease from Trypanosoma cruzi is common in developing countries per the lecture, not developed countries.

options.text: Rheumatic fever due to group A streptococcal infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Rheumatic carditis is historically important but is not listed as the most common cause in developed countries in the lecture.

options.text: Tuberculous pericarditis causing myocardial infiltration
options.rationale: Wrong: TB-related cardiac disease is not listed as a leading cause of myocarditis in developed countries in the lecture.

options.text: Fungal myocarditis from endemic dimorphic fungi exposure
options.rationale: Wrong: Fungal causes are rare and not listed among the common causes in developed countries per the lecture.

question: A patient with acute pericarditis is treated with high-dose NSAIDs and colchicine. Which cellular or pharmacologic mechanism best explains colchicine's role in reducing recurrence?

options.text: Inhibition of microtubule polymerization reducing neutrophil activity
options.rationale: Correct: Colchicine acts by inhibiting microtubule assembly and neutrophil function, which reduces pericardial inflammation and recurrence as discussed in the lecture.

options.text: Direct cyclooxygenase inhibition decreasing prostaglandin synthesis
options.rationale: Wrong: COX inhibition describes NSAIDs, not colchicine; this would be correct only if colchicine were a COX inhibitor.

options.text: Blockade of interleukin 6 receptor signaling to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-1 or IL-6 blockade is a different mechanism; this would be correct only if colchicine acted on cytokine receptors as described.

options.text: Neutralization of circulating viral particles preventing infection
options.rationale: Wrong: Colchicine is not an antiviral; it would be correct only if the drug had direct antiviral properties.

options.text: Upregulation of corticosteroid receptors enhancing steroid response
options.rationale: Wrong: Colchicine does not upregulate steroid receptors; this would be correct only if colchicine modified steroid signaling per lecture evidence.

question: A 33-year-old man with pleuritic chest pain and a scratchy sound on auscultation has normal troponins and negative pulmonary CTA. Which next step aligns with the lecture's recommended immediate management in the emergency setting?

options.text: Administer intravenous NSAID and arrange short observation
options.rationale: Correct: The case described IV ketorolac in ED and 24-hour observation with telemetry before discharge, per the lecture.

options.text: Start high-dose intravenous corticosteroids immediately
options.rationale: Wrong: Steroids are reserved for connective tissue or uremic causes; immediate steroids would be appropriate only if such etiologies were present.

options.text: Proceed directly to emergent pericardiocentesis without imaging
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericardiocentesis is for hemodynamically significant effusion or tamponade; it would be correct only if echo showed tamponade physiology.

options.text: Begin empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for bacterial pericarditis
options.rationale: Wrong: Antibiotics are indicated only with suspected bacterial etiology; empiric antibiotics are not routine for presumed viral pericarditis.

options.text: Discharge home without therapy and no follow-up arranged
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture recommends observation and anti-inflammatory therapy; discharge without treatment would be appropriate only if symptoms resolved and diagnosis excluded.

question: A patient with recurrent symptomatic pericardial effusions refractory to medical therapy is being considered for an invasive procedure. According to the lecture, which surgical option is indicated for symptomatic, recurrent effusions or suspected neoplastic etiology?

options.text: Pericardial window creation by cardiothoracic surgery for drainage
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists pericardial window and pericardiectomy as surgical options for recurrent symptomatic effusions or suspected neoplastic/bacterial etiologies.

options.text: Routine thoracentesis to remove pleural fluid for symptom relief
options.rationale: Wrong: Thoracentesis treats pleural effusion, not pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if pleural fluid were the primary problem.

options.text: Immediate heart transplantation for recurrent pericardial effusions
options.rationale: Wrong: Transplantation is for end-stage myocardial disease, not recurrent pericardial effusion; it would be correct only with irreversible myocardial failure.

options.text: Percutaneous coronary intervention to treat presumed ischemia
options.rationale: Wrong: PCI addresses coronary obstruction, not pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if ischemia were the underlying cause.

options.text: Placement of an indwelling pleural catheter for chronic drainage
options.rationale: Wrong: Indwelling pleural catheters manage pleural effusions, not pericardial effusions; it would be correct only if pleural effusion predominated.

question: Which laboratory marker is recommended to follow until normalization before allowing return to strenuous activity after pericardial inflammation, per the lecture guidance?

options.text: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein monitored until normalization
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture advises activity restriction until symptom resolution or normalization of hs-CRP.

options.text: Serial hemoglobin concentration to assess bleeding risk
options.rationale: Wrong: Hemoglobin is not cited as a marker for activity clearance in pericarditis; it would be correct only if anemia or bleeding were a concern.

options.text: Fasting lipid panel to evaluate cardiovascular risk profile
options.rationale: Wrong: Lipid panels are not used to time return to activity after pericarditis; they would be relevant only for long-term risk management.

options.text: Serum creatinine to determine renal dosing of colchicine
options.rationale: Wrong: While renal function affects dosing, the lecture specifically mentions hs-CRP normalization for activity clearance; creatinine would be correct only for dosing adjustments.

options.text: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate as sole determinant for activity resumption
options.rationale: Wrong: ESR is not specified as the primary marker; the lecture highlights hs-CRP rather than ESR for monitoring resolution.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis has non-specific ST-T changes and occasional premature ventricular complexes on ECG. According to the lecture, which percentage of myocarditis cases typically show elevated cardiac troponin I?

options.text: Approximately thirty-five percent of myocarditis cases show elevation
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture cites that hs-troponin I is elevated in about 35% of myocarditis cases.

options.text: Nearly one hundred percent of myocarditis cases show elevation
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture reports only ~35% elevation; 100% would be correct only if all cases had myocardial necrosis detectable by troponin.

options.text: Less than five percent of myocarditis cases show elevation
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture gives a much higher figure (~35%);  38ºC or signs of sepsis to assess for bacterial etiology.

options.text: Defer cultures and start colchicine immediately without testing
options.rationale: Wrong: Empiric colchicine without cultures would miss bacterial causes; cultures are indicated when fever or sepsis is present.

options.text: Order only ANA testing and ignore infectious workup
options.rationale: Wrong: ANA is for autoimmune evaluation but infectious workup including cultures is prioritized in febrile or septic patients.

options.text: Perform immediate pericardiectomy without microbiologic evaluation
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgery is reserved for specific indications; microbiologic evaluation is necessary before invasive interventions when infection is suspected.

options.text: Obtain urine culture only as the sole infectious test
options.rationale: Wrong: Urine culture alone is insufficient to evaluate suspected bacterial pericarditis; blood cultures are specifically recommended.

question: A patient with chest pain and diffuse ST elevation is found to have a small pericardial effusion on echo without hemodynamic compromise. According to the lecture, which management strategy is most appropriate initially?

options.text: Treat with NSAIDs and colchicine and observe clinically
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends NSAIDs plus colchicine for most acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis and observation when effusion is not hemodynamically significant.

options.text: Immediate pericardiocentesis to evacuate small asymptomatic effusion
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericardiocentesis is for hemodynamically significant effusions or tamponade; it would be correct only if signs of compromise developed.

options.text: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed bacterial pericarditis
options.rationale: Wrong: Antibiotics are indicated only with suspected bacterial etiology; empiric antibiotics are not routine for small, likely viral effusions.

options.text: Begin high-dose corticosteroids as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Steroids are reserved for specific causes like connective tissue disease; they would be correct only if such an etiology were identified.

options.text: Discharge without therapy and no outpatient follow-up arranged
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture recommends anti-inflammatory therapy and follow-up; discharge without treatment would be inappropriate unless diagnosis excluded.

question: Which of the following best characterizes the natural history of most patients with acute myocarditis presenting with dilated cardiomyopathy, according to the lecture?

options.text: Most patients have partial or full clinical recovery with treatment
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states most patients recover partially or fully; only a small percentage progress to fulminant disease requiring transplant.

options.text: Nearly all patients progress rapidly to heart transplantation
options.rationale: Wrong: Only a small percentage progress to transplant; universal progression is not supported by the lecture.

options.text: Chronic progressive decline without any chance of recovery
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture indicates many recover; chronic irreversible decline is not the typical course.

options.text: Immediate development of constrictive physiology in most cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Constrictive pericarditis is a pericardial complication and not the usual outcome of myocarditis; it would be correct only with specific pericardial involvement.

options.text: Spontaneous resolution without any medical therapy in all patients
options.rationale: Wrong: While some recover, the lecture recommends medical therapy and follow-up; assuming universal spontaneous resolution contradicts guidance.

question: A patient with suspected pericarditis has chest pain worse when supine and improved when sitting up. Which feature of the pain is most characteristic per the lecture's description?
cited_learning_objective: Acute Pericarditis – Diagnostic Criteria (Need 2 out of 4)

options.text: Sharp pleuritic chest pain improved by sitting upright and leaning forward
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes pericarditis chest pain as sharp, pleuritic, and improved by sitting up and leaning forward.

options.text: Dull constant chest pressure worse with exertion and rest
options.rationale: Wrong: Ischemic chest pain is often exertional and pressure-like; pericarditis pain is pleuritic and positional.

options.text: Intermittent stabbing pain reproducible by chest wall palpation
options.rationale: Wrong: Musculoskeletal pain is reproducible with palpation; pericardial pain is not typically reproducible by palpation.

options.text: Burning retrosternal pain relieved by antacids and meals
options.rationale: Wrong: Esophageal or reflux pain is relieved by antacids; this pattern does not match pericarditis features.

options.text: Left-sided pleuritic pain with pleural friction rub on auscultation
options.rationale: Wrong: Pleural friction rub suggests pleuritis; pericardial friction rub is superficial and best heard at left sternal border and positional.

question: Which of the following is an indication for pericardial drainage listed in the lecture beyond tamponade physiology?

options.text: Suspicion of neoplastic or bacterial etiology with moderate to large effusion
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists suspicion of neoplastic or bacterial etiology with moderate to large effusion as an indication for drainage.

options.text: Small asymptomatic effusion discovered incidentally on imaging
options.rationale: Wrong: Small asymptomatic effusions typically do not require drainage; drainage would be correct only if symptoms or hemodynamic compromise developed.

options.text: Isolated pericardial calcification without effusion
options.rationale: Wrong: Calcification alone is not an indication for drainage; it would be correct only if constrictive physiology or symptomatic effusion were present.

options.text: Mild chest pain responsive to NSAIDs and colchicine
options.rationale: Wrong: Symptom control with medical therapy obviates drainage; drainage would be correct only if refractory symptoms persisted with effusion.

options.text: Stable chronic pericardial effusion with normal hemodynamics
options.rationale: Wrong: Stable effusions without symptoms or hemodynamic impact are not immediate indications for drainage per the lecture.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis has ventricular arrhythmias and reduced LVEF. Which specific myocarditis subtype mentioned in the lecture is associated with improved survival when treated with cyclosporine plus prednisone?

options.text: Giant cell myocarditis treated with cyclosporine and prednisone
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes improved survival in giant cell myocarditis with cyclosporine and prednisone therapy.

options.text: Lymphocytic myocarditis treated with high-dose steroids alone
options.rationale: Wrong: Lymphocytic myocarditis may be treated differently and antivirals are discussed; steroids alone are not the specific cyclosporine regimen cited for giant cell disease.

options.text: Eosinophilic myocarditis treated with antiviral ribavirin therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Eosinophilic myocarditis is treated with high-dose steroids per the lecture; antivirals would be correct only if viral eosinophilic overlap were proven.

options.text: Sarcoid myocarditis treated exclusively with colchicine therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Sarcoid myocarditis is treated with high-dose steroids, not colchicine; colchicine is for pericarditis recurrence prevention.

options.text: Viral enteroviral myocarditis treated with cyclosporine routinely
options.rationale: Wrong: Cyclosporine is indicated for giant cell myocarditis; routine use in viral enteroviral myocarditis is not supported by the lecture.

question: A patient with acute pericarditis is intolerant of NSAIDs. According to the lecture, which alternative medication class is reserved for specific etiologies rather than routine use?

options.text: Systemic corticosteroids reserved for connective tissue or uremic causes
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states steroids are usually only for pericarditis caused by connective tissue disorders or uremia.

options.text: Long-term colchicine monotherapy for all NSAID-intolerant patients
options.rationale: Wrong: While colchicine is used, steroids are the class reserved for specific etiologies; colchicine monotherapy is not the reserved alternative described.

options.text: Routine intravenous antibiotics for all NSAID-intolerant cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Antibiotics are for suspected bacterial causes, not a general alternative to NSAIDs; they would be correct only with bacterial suspicion.

options.text: Immediate surgical pericardiectomy as first-line alternative therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgery is reserved for refractory or constrictive disease; it is not the routine alternative to NSAIDs.

options.text: High-dose opioid analgesia as disease-modifying therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Opioids treat pain but do not modify pericardial inflammation; they would be correct only for symptomatic analgesia, not disease control.

question: A patient with suspected pericarditis has a normal chest radiograph. Which chest x-ray finding described in the lecture would suggest a large pericardial effusion instead?

options.text: Enlarged cardiac silhouette consistent with moderate to large effusion
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture shows that a pericardial effusion can produce an enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest x-ray.

options.text: Focal lobar consolidation indicating bacterial pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong: Lobar consolidation suggests pneumonia, not pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if concomitant pneumonia existed.

options.text: Hyperinflated lungs typical of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Hyperinflation is a pulmonary finding unrelated to pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if COPD were present.

options.text: Mediastinal widening specific for pulmonary embolism diagnosis
options.rationale: Wrong: Mediastinal widening suggests aortic pathology or mass, not specifically PE; it would be correct only if imaging and clinical context supported it.

options.text: Small unilateral pleural effusion without cardiac enlargement
options.rationale: Wrong: A small pleural effusion without cardiac enlargement does not indicate a large pericardial effusion; it would be correct only if pericardial fluid were minimal.

question: A patient with chest pain and pericardial friction rub is treated and symptom-free at six weeks. According to the lecture case outcome, which follow-up finding is most consistent with that scenario?

options.text: No recurrence of symptoms and normal transthoracic echocardiogram
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture case reported no recurrence at six-week follow-up and a normal echocardiogram.

options.text: Progressive constrictive physiology requiring pericardiectomy
options.rationale: Wrong: The case resolved without progression; constrictive physiology would be correct only if chronic constriction developed.

options.text: Development of persistent high-degree atrioventricular block
options.rationale: Wrong: The case did not develop high-degree AV block; that would be correct only if conduction system involvement occurred.

options.text: New large pericardial effusion necessitating urgent drainage
options.rationale: Wrong: The case had normal echo and no recurrence; urgent drainage would be correct only if a large symptomatic effusion developed.

options.text: Chronic daily fevers and progressive leukocytosis despite therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: The case improved clinically; persistent fever and leukocytosis would indicate ongoing infection or inflammation contrary to the reported outcome.

question: Which of the following best summarizes the lecture's guidance on NSAID use in myocarditis compared with pericarditis?

options.text: NSAIDs are avoided in myocarditis and used in pericarditis
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture advises NSAIDs are usually not effective and may worsen myonecrosis in myocarditis, whereas they are first-line in pericarditis.

options.text: NSAIDs are first-line therapy for both myocarditis and pericarditis
options.rationale: Wrong: NSAIDs are recommended for pericarditis but generally avoided in myocarditis per the lecture; blanket first-line use is incorrect.

options.text: NSAIDs are contraindicated in pericarditis but indicated in myocarditis
options.rationale: Wrong: This reverses the lecture guidance; NSAIDs are indicated in pericarditis and usually avoided in myocarditis.

options.text: NSAIDs have no role in either pericarditis or myocarditis management
options.rationale: Wrong: NSAIDs play a central role in pericarditis management per the lecture; claiming no role contradicts that guidance.

options.text: NSAIDs should be replaced by antibiotics in all inflammatory cardiac disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Antibiotics are for bacterial infections only; they are not a universal replacement for NSAIDs in inflammatory cardiac conditions.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis is being evaluated for anticoagulation. According to the lecture, which finding would most strongly support initiating anticoagulation?

options.text: Dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction below thirty-five percent
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture suggests considering anticoagulation if LV dilation with LVEF <35%, AF, or LV thrombus is present.

options.text: Mild pericardial effusion without ventricular dysfunction
options.rationale: Wrong: Small effusion alone does not indicate anticoagulation; anticoagulation would be correct only with thrombus or severe LV dysfunction.

options.text: Isolated premature ventricular complexes on ambulatory monitoring
options.rationale: Wrong: PVCs alone do not mandate anticoagulation; anticoagulation would be correct only if thromboembolic risk factors were present.

options.text: Elevated hs-CRP without structural heart disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Inflammation markers alone do not justify anticoagulation; structural findings like low EF or thrombus are required.

options.text: Transient chest pain resolved with NSAIDs and colchicine
options.rationale: Wrong: Symptom resolution does not indicate need for anticoagulation; anticoagulation would be correct only with objective thrombotic risk.

question: A patient with suspected pericarditis has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus. According to the lecture, which anti-inflammatory agent class is more likely to be used in this context rather than routine cases?

options.text: Systemic corticosteroids for connective tissue disease associated pericarditis
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states steroids are usually used in pericarditis caused by connective tissue disorders such as SLE.

options.text: Long-term NSAID monotherapy without adjunctive colchicine
options.rationale: Wrong: While NSAIDs are used, steroids are specifically indicated for connective tissue disease; NSAID monotherapy would be correct only if steroids were contraindicated.

options.text: Immediate pericardiectomy as first-line therapy for SLE pericarditis
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgery is reserved for refractory or constrictive disease; it would be correct only if medical therapy failed.

options.text: Routine antiviral therapy for all autoimmune pericarditis cases
options.rationale: Wrong: Antivirals are for viral etiologies; autoimmune pericarditis is treated with immunomodulation like steroids, not routine antivirals.

options.text: High-dose colchicine monotherapy replacing steroids entirely
options.rationale: Wrong: Colchicine reduces recurrence but steroids are indicated for autoimmune causes; colchicine alone would be correct only if steroids were contraindicated.

question: A patient with chest pain and diffuse ST elevation is found to have pericardial friction rub and elevated white-cell count. Which of the following combinations of tests from the lecture is most appropriate for initial evaluation?

options.text: History physical ECG chest x-ray CBC troponins CRP and echo
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends history, exam, 12-lead ECG, chest x-ray, CBC, cardiac biomarkers, hs-CRP, and echocardiography as part of evaluation.

options.text: Immediate cardiac MRI CT coronary angiography and endomyocardial biopsy
options.rationale: Wrong: MRI, CT, cath, and EMB are selective or advanced tests; initial evaluation per the lecture includes ECG, labs, CXR, and echo.

options.text: Only chest x-ray and empiric antibiotics without cardiac testing
options.rationale: Wrong: Empiric antibiotics without cardiac evaluation is inappropriate; the lecture emphasizes cardiac-focused testing.

options.text: Urine toxicology and pulmonary function testing as first-line
options.rationale: Wrong: These are not primary initial tests for suspected pericarditis; they would be correct only if alternative diagnoses were suspected.

options.text: Immediate surgical exploration without noninvasive assessment
options.rationale: Wrong: Surgery is not the initial step; noninvasive assessment including echo is recommended first per the lecture.

question: A patient with suspected pericarditis reports recent mRNA COVID vaccination six months ago and denies recent infection. According to the lecture, how should the clinician interpret vaccine timing relative to pericardial disease risk?

options.text: mRNA vaccine associated myocarditis is very rare and timing matters
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes myocarditis/pericarditis after mRNA COVID vaccines is very rare and most reports occurred in younger individuals, with timing relevant to causality assessment.

options.text: Any mRNA vaccine received at any time guarantees pericarditis diagnosis
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture emphasizes rarity and does not state vaccination guarantees disease; causality depends on timing and clinical correlation.

options.text: mRNA vaccines are the most common cause of pericarditis in adults
options.rationale: Wrong: The lecture lists viral causes as common; vaccines are described as very rare causes, not the most common.

options.text: Vaccination history is irrelevant to pericarditis evaluation
options.rationale: Wrong: Vaccination history can be relevant though rare; dismissing it entirely contradicts the lecture's discussion.

options.text: mRNA vaccine within six months always excludes viral etiology
options.rationale: Wrong: Recent vaccination does not exclude viral causes; etiologic assessment requires full clinical evaluation.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis has new high-degree atrioventricular block on ECG. According to the lecture, which diagnostic consideration should be high on the differential because it may require specific therapy?
cited_learning_objective: When should Endomyocardial Biopsy (EMB) be performed?

options.text: Cardiac sarcoidosis causing conduction system involvement treatable with steroids
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists sarcoid myocarditis as an important EMB diagnosis; sarcoid can cause high-degree AV block and may respond to high-dose steroids.

options.text: Ischemic conduction disease from chronic coronary artery disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Ischemic disease can cause conduction abnormalities but EMB-targeted sarcoidosis is more likely when AV block accompanies myocarditis; ischemia would be correct only with coronary findings.

options.text: Benign vagally mediated transient AV block resolving without therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Transient vagal AV block is less likely in the setting of myocarditis and hemodynamic compromise; it would be correct only if clinical context supported vagal etiology.

options.text: Medication-induced AV block from recent beta-blocker initiation
options.rationale: Wrong: Drug-induced block is possible but EMB diagnoses like sarcoid are prioritized when myocarditis and AV block coexist; medication cause would be correct only if temporal drug exposure matched onset.

options.text: Congenital complete heart block present since birth
options.rationale: Wrong: Congenital block would not present acutely with myocarditis; it would be correct only if lifelong history indicated congenital disease.

question: A patient with recurrent pericarditis refractory to colchicine and steroids is being considered for advanced therapy. According to the lecture, which class of agents is described as a newer option to prevent pericardiectomy?

options.text: Anti-interleukin 1 biologic agents for refractory pericarditis management
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture mentions new anti-IL1 agents can help prevent pericardiectomy in refractory cases.

options.text: Long-term high-dose NSAIDs as the newest advanced therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: NSAIDs are standard therapy, not the novel agents described; anti-IL1 agents are the newer option per the lecture.

options.text: Routine use of intravenous immunoglobulin for all recurrent cases
options.rationale: Wrong: IVIG is not cited as the new standard; anti-IL1 agents are specifically mentioned for refractory disease.

options.text: Chronic antibiotic suppression to prevent inflammatory recurrence
options.rationale: Wrong: Antibiotics are for bacterial etiologies, not a preventive strategy for idiopathic recurrent pericarditis; anti-IL1 agents are the targeted therapy discussed.

options.text: Immediate pericardiectomy as the preferred first-line for refractory disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericardiectomy is a last-resort surgical option; the lecture highlights anti-IL1 agents as a medical alternative to avoid surgery.

question: A patient with suspected pericarditis has leukocytosis and elevated hs-CRP. Which of the following best describes the role of hs-CRP in management according to the lecture?

options.text: Use hs-CRP to monitor inflammation and guide activity restriction timing
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends restricting activity until symptoms resolve or hs-CRP normalizes, indicating its role in monitoring.

options.text: Use hs-CRP to diagnose bacterial pericarditis exclusively
options.rationale: Wrong: hs-CRP is a nonspecific inflammation marker and not exclusive for bacterial diagnosis; cultures are needed for bacterial confirmation.

options.text: Use hs-CRP to determine colchicine dosing precisely
options.rationale: Wrong: Colchicine dosing is not titrated to hs-CRP per the lecture; dosing follows standard regimens and clinical response.

options.text: Use hs-CRP to replace echocardiography for effusion assessment
options.rationale: Wrong: Echo is required to assess effusion; hs-CRP cannot substitute for imaging evaluation.

options.text: Use hs-CRP to decide immediate need for pericardiocentesis
options.rationale: Wrong: Hemodynamic signs and echo findings determine need for pericardiocentesis; hs-CRP alone does not dictate drainage.

question: A patient with suspected pericarditis has a negative pulmonary CTA and no JVD but a pericardial friction rub. Which feature in the lecture differentiates pericardial tamponade from uncomplicated effusion on exam?

options.text: Presence of pulsus paradoxus and jugular venous distention in tamponade
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes pulsus paradoxus and JVD are exam findings associated with tamponade, which were absent in the case without tamponade.

options.text: Loud pericardial friction rub indicates tamponade always
options.rationale: Wrong: Friction rub indicates pericardial inflammation but does not by itself indicate tamponade; tamponade requires hemodynamic compromise.

options.text: Normal carotid upstrokes confirm presence of tamponade
options.rationale: Wrong: Normal carotid upstrokes do not confirm tamponade; tamponade often shows diminished pulses and other signs.

options.text: Elevated respiratory rate alone is diagnostic of tamponade
options.rationale: Wrong: Tachypnea is nonspecific and not diagnostic of tamponade; hemodynamic signs and echo are required.

options.text: Low-grade fever is the most specific sign of tamponade
options.rationale: Wrong: Fever is nonspecific and not specific for tamponade; it may accompany inflammatory conditions but does not indicate tamponade.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis is found to have dilated LV and LV mural thrombus on echo. According to the lecture, which management step should be considered?

options.text: Initiate anticoagulation to reduce embolic risk from mural thrombus
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture recommends considering anticoagulation if LV mural thrombus, AF, or LVEF <35% is present.

options.text: Stop all heart failure medications and observe without therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Stopping HF therapy is inappropriate; anticoagulation and GDMT are indicated when thrombus and dysfunction are present.

options.text: Perform immediate pericardiectomy to remove thrombus
options.rationale: Wrong: Pericardiectomy does not address intracavitary LV thrombus; surgical thrombectomy would be considered only in select cases.

options.text: Treat with colchicine alone to dissolve intracardiac thrombus
options.rationale: Wrong: Colchicine reduces pericardial inflammation but does not dissolve thrombus; anticoagulation is the indicated therapy.

options.text: Administer high-dose NSAIDs to rapidly lyse mural thrombus
options.rationale: Wrong: NSAIDs do not lyse thrombus; anticoagulation or surgical approaches are required for mural thrombus management.
